title: PARITY-B6: Verify RETURNING clause emits correct IPK values after fix
close_reason: Merged into B5 (bd-3l6e): RETURNING verification is a test concern, absorbed into the comprehensive test suite. All RETURNING test cases added to B5.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# PARITY-B6: Verify RETURNING clause emits correct IPK values after fix

## Context

The RETURNING clause on INSERT must reflect the actual rowid used, not the auto-generated one.
This was the original symptom that exposed the IPK bug:

```sql
INSERT INTO t VALUES (42, 'test') RETURNING id;
-- Currently returns: Integer(1)  ← WRONG (auto-generated rowid)
-- Should return:     Integer(42) ← user-supplied IPK value
```

## Why This Needs Separate Verification

RETURNING is compiled AFTER the Insert opcode. The RETURNING codegen reads column values from
the cursor that was just written to. For IPK columns, it should emit `Opcode::Rowid` (just like
SELECT does for IPK columns).

The key question: does the RETURNING codegen already handle IPK correctly (using Rowid opcode
for IPK columns), or does it use Column opcode which would read from the record body?

## What to Verify

1. **Check RETURNING codegen** in `codegen.rs` — search for where RETURNING columns are compiled.
   Verify it uses the same IPK-aware Column/Rowid dispatch as SELECT does.

2. **If RETURNING already uses Rowid opcode**: The fix in B1 (putting the correct value into the
   rowid) should automatically fix RETURNING. Just verify with tests.

3. **If RETURNING uses Column opcode**: Since we keep IPK in the record (Approach B), the Column
   opcode would read the stored value, which after the B1 fix should be correct (we copy the
   user value or the generated rowid into the IPK record position).

Either way, RETURNING should work after B1's fix. This bead is a verification checkpoint.

## Test Cases

```sql
-- All should return correct IPK values:
INSERT INTO t VALUES (42, 'test') RETURNING id;          -- 42
INSERT INTO t VALUES (42, 'test') RETURNING *;           -- 42, 'test'
INSERT INTO t VALUES (42, 'test') RETURNING rowid;       -- 42
INSERT INTO t VALUES (42, 'test') RETURNING id, rowid;   -- 42, 42 (same value)
INSERT INTO t VALUES (NULL, 'test') RETURNING id;        -- auto-generated
INSERT INTO t(name) VALUES ('test') RETURNING id;        -- auto-generated

-- Multi-row:
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1,'a'),(2,'b') RETURNING id;       -- 1, 2

-- UPDATE with RETURNING (separate but related):
UPDATE t SET name='y' WHERE id=42 RETURNING id;          -- 42
DELETE FROM t WHERE id=42 RETURNING id;                   -- 42
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- `probe_insert_returning_rowid` test passes (the original failing test)
- `probe_insert_returning_columns` continues to pass
- `probe_insert_returning_multi_row` continues to pass
- `probe_update_returning_star` continues to pass
- New RETURNING+IPK tests pass (if not already covered by B5)

## Dependencies

Blocked by B1 (bd-13b8) — the core fix must land first. This is verification only.

title: Testing & Fault Injection
description:
Comprehensive testing and fault injection suite for FrankenSQLite. This epic covers adversarial testing scenarios that exercise failure modes not covered by unit or integration tests. The goal is to prove that FrankenSQLite maintains correctness and durability under every imaginable failure scenario.

## Philosophy
Normal tests verify that things work when everything goes right. Fault injection tests verify that things work when everything goes wrong. For a database that claims self-healing durability and serializable isolation, fault injection is not optional — it is the primary evidence that the claims are true.

## Coverage
- Storage layer: corruption, torn writes, crash during compaction
- Concurrency: lock contention, skewed distributions, SSI validation under adversarial schedules
- Durability: RaptorQ self-healing under realistic corruption scenarios
- Conformance: SQLite TCL test harness for compatibility

## Connection to Other Features
- RaptorQ self-healing is validated by corruption fault injection
- SSI correctness is validated by adversarial concurrency schedules
- Buffer pool correctness is validated by resize storms
- WAL correctness is validated by crash-during-write scenarios

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All fault injection scenarios implemented and passing
- [ ] E2E tests for SSI and RaptorQ under adversarial conditions
- [ ] SQLite TCL test harness running and tracked
- [ ] CI integration for critical fault injection tests
- [ ] No silent data corruption under any tested scenario

## Success Criteria
Epic completion requires all child beads to satisfy their structured acceptance criteria, including explicit unit/property coverage, deterministic e2e evidence, and structured logging/metrics validation.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Every child bead in this epic defines concrete unit/property test scope with deterministic pass/fail thresholds and invariant IDs. 2. Critical-path end-to-end scenarios are implemented as reproducible e2e scripts (fixed seeds, replay commands, artifact bundles) across happy-path and adversarial-path behavior. 3. Structured logging and metrics contracts are mandatory for all child outputs (trace_id, run_id, scenario_id, seed, timing, outcome, error context) and validated by CI conformance checks. 4. Epic completion requires a machine-readable evidence manifest linking child unit/e2e/log artifacts to acceptance outcomes, plus an explicit fallback/rollback plan that preserves concurrent-writer defaults.

title: Fault injection: skewed key distributions
description:
Fault injection test with skewed key distributions that stress B-tree, buffer pool, and MVCC version chain hot spots. Skewed distributions expose bugs that uniform random testing misses.

Distributions:
1. Zipfian (s=1.0): 20% of keys receive 80% of accesses. Tests buffer pool hot-page behavior and version chain length on hot pages.
2. Zipfian (s=2.0): extreme skew, 5% of keys receive 95% of accesses. Tests EBR under extreme chain lengths.
3. Sequential monotonic: all inserts to the rightmost B-tree leaf. Tests B-tree split behavior and page split storms.
4. Reverse sequential: all inserts to the leftmost leaf. Same split stress in opposite direction.
5. Hot-cold: 100 hot keys (99% of accesses) + 10000 cold keys (1%). Tests buffer pool eviction under extreme working set mismatch.

For each distribution, exercise:
- INSERT workload: 1M inserts
- UPDATE workload: 1M updates to existing keys
- Mixed: 50% insert + 50% update
- Concurrent: 32 threads with same distribution

Verification:
- No crashes or panics
- All committed data readable and correct
- Buffer pool hit rate documented (expected: very high for hot keys, very low for cold keys)
- Version chain lengths bounded by EBR
- B-tree structure valid (no corruption, balanced)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 5 distributions tested with all 4 workload types
- [ ] No crashes, panics, or data corruption
- [ ] Concurrent workloads complete without deadlock
- [ ] Version chain lengths bounded
- [ ] B-tree integrity verified after each workload
- [ ] Results documented with distribution-specific analysis

title: Fault injection: resize storms
description:
Fault injection test for buffer pool resize storms — rapidly changing buffer pool size to stress the eviction, swizzling, and MVCC machinery. Resize storms expose race conditions in buffer management that normal workloads rarely trigger.

Scenarios:
1. Rapid shrink: reduce buffer pool from 1000 pages to 10 pages in 100ms steps (eviction storm)
2. Rapid grow: increase buffer pool from 10 pages to 1000 pages in 100ms steps
3. Oscillation: alternate between 10 and 1000 pages every 50ms for 10 seconds
4. Concurrent resize + queries: resize buffer pool while running TPC-H Q1 (scan-heavy)
5. Concurrent resize + writes: resize while 32 writers are actively inserting

Verification:
- No crashes or panics during resize
- No use-after-free (evicted page frames not accessed after free)
- No deadlock between resize and page access
- Query results correct during and after resize
- Buffer pool size accurately reflects the configured size at quiescence

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 5 scenarios pass
- [ ] No crashes, deadlocks, or use-after-free
- [ ] Query results correct during resize
- [ ] AddressSanitizer clean
- [ ] Resize completes within bounded time (no starvation)

title: Fault injection: crash during compaction
description:
Fault injection test for crash during compaction (checkpoint) operations. Compaction is one of the most dangerous operations — it moves data between WAL and main database file. A crash during compaction can corrupt the database if recovery is not handled correctly.

Scenarios:
1. Crash during WAL checkpoint (wal_checkpoint): inject crash at random point during page writeback
2. Crash after partial page write (torn write): write half of a 4KB page, then crash
3. Crash during B-tree rebalance: inject crash during B-tree node split/merge
4. Crash during VACUUM: inject crash while reorganizing pages
5. Power loss simulation: kill process with SIGKILL at random intervals during compaction

Implementation:
- Use failpoints (fail crate or custom) to inject crashes at specific code locations
- Simulate torn writes by truncating file at random byte offset within a page
- After crash injection, restart database and verify recovery
- Recovery must produce a consistent database (no corruption, no missing committed data)

Verification after recovery:
- Database passes integrity check (PRAGMA integrity_check equivalent)
- All committed transactions are present
- No uncommitted transaction data is visible
- WAL is either empty (fully checkpointed) or contains valid redo records
- B-tree structure is valid

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 5 crash scenarios implemented with failpoints
- [ ] Recovery succeeds in all scenarios (consistent database after restart)
- [ ] No committed data lost
- [ ] No uncommitted data visible
- [ ] B-tree integrity verified after recovery
- [ ] 100 randomized crash points per scenario (statistical coverage)
- [ ] CI integration (run nightly due to time cost)

title: Fault injection: lock contention storms
description:
Fault injection test for extreme lock contention scenarios. With page-level MVCC and SSI, lock contention manifests differently than in traditional databases — instead of deadlocks, we see SSI abort storms. This test validates that the system remains available under extreme contention.

Scenarios:
1. Single hot row: 100 threads all update the same row concurrently (maximum SSI conflict rate)
2. Hot page: 100 threads update different rows on the same page (page-level MVCC contention)
3. Lock convoy: one slow transaction holds a page while 100 fast transactions queue behind it
4. Abort storm: deliberate write-skew patterns that cause 90%+ of transactions to abort
5. Priority inversion: high-priority read transaction blocked by low-priority writer holding epoch pin

Metrics to capture:
- Abort rate (should be bounded, not 100% for scenarios 1-3)
- Throughput under contention (operations/second, should not go to zero)
- p99 latency under contention (should be bounded, not infinite)
- Livelock detection: if forward progress stalls for > 10 seconds, flag as livelock
- Memory usage: SSI conflict tracking under high abort rates

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 5 scenarios complete without deadlock or livelock
- [ ] Forward progress guaranteed (at least 1 transaction commits per second)
- [ ] Abort rate bounded and documented for each scenario
- [ ] p99 latency bounded and documented
- [ ] No memory leak from aborted transaction state
- [ ] Livelock detection mechanism works

title: E2E test: SSI serialization correctness under 100 concurrent writers
description:
End-to-end test that validates SSI serialization correctness under 100 concurrent writers with a serialization checker. This is the definitive proof that page-level MVCC + SSI provides true serializable isolation.

Test design:
1. Create a database with a known initial state (e.g., bank accounts with known balances, invariant: sum of all balances = constant)
2. Launch 100 writer threads, each executing random transfer transactions (read two accounts, check constraint, write two accounts)
3. Each transaction either commits or aborts (SSI may abort for write-skew prevention)
4. After all transactions complete, verify:
   a. Sum of all balances == initial sum (invariant preserved)
   b. No negative balances if constraint was always checked
   c. Committed transaction history forms a valid serializable schedule

Serialization checker:
- Record all committed transactions with their read-sets and write-sets
- Use a cycle-detection algorithm on the serialization graph
- If a cycle exists among committed transactions: SSI BUG — serialization anomaly was allowed
- The checker is a separate validation tool, not part of the database itself

Run configuration:
- 100 writers, 10000 transactions each
- Transaction types: transfer (read 2, write 2), deposit (read 1, write 1), balance check (read all)
- Mix: 70% transfer, 20% deposit, 10% balance check
- Duration: 60 seconds minimum

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] 100 concurrent writers complete without deadlock
- [ ] Global invariant (sum of balances) preserved at all times
- [ ] Serialization checker finds ZERO cycles among committed transactions
- [ ] Abort rate < 20% (SSI is not overly conservative)
- [ ] Throughput > 1000 committed transactions/second
- [ ] Test runs in CI (reduced scale: 10 writers, 1000 transactions)

title: E2E test: RaptorQ self-healing with 5% random page corruption
description:
End-to-end test that validates RaptorQ self-healing by corrupting 5% of database pages randomly and verifying automatic repair. This is the showcase test for FrankenSQLite's core differentiator.

Test procedure:
1. Create database with known data (1000 rows across multiple tables, known checksums)
2. Run normal workload to populate WAL and trigger checkpoint (ensures repair symbols exist)
3. Close database cleanly
4. Corrupt 5% of pages: for each target page, flip random bits (1-8 bits per page)
5. Open database
6. Read all rows (this triggers corruption detection via BLAKE3 checksum mismatch)
7. Verify: all rows read correctly (RaptorQ repair transparent to reader)
8. Verify: evidence ledger contains repair records for each corrupted page
9. Verify: BLAKE3 witness proofs in evidence ledger are valid
10. Close and reopen database: corrupted pages should be permanently repaired (not just cached)

Corruption variants:
- Random bit flips (simulating cosmic rays / bit rot)
- Zero-fill (simulating sector failure)
- Random data overwrite (simulating stray writes)
- Header corruption (page header fields)

Expected results:
- 5% corruption with 50% repair symbol overhead: 100% repair success
- 10% corruption with 50% repair symbol overhead: should still succeed (margin)
- 20% corruption: may exceed repair capacity, test graceful degradation

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] 5% random corruption fully repaired (zero data loss)
- [ ] All corruption variants tested
- [ ] Evidence ledger entries for every repair
- [ ] BLAKE3 witness proofs valid
- [ ] Permanent repair (persisted, not just cached)
- [ ] Graceful degradation when repair capacity exceeded
- [ ] Test runs in CI (< 30 seconds)

## Task: TUI framework setup with frankentui and channel-based data feed

### What
Set up the TUI binary and core infrastructure using frankentui (at /dp/frankentui), with a channel-based architecture that allows background test threads to feed data to the UI.

### Architecture
```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Background Threads                               │
│  ┌─────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  │
│  │Benchmark │  │Corruption│  │  Correctness   │  │
│  │ Runner   │  │ Recovery │  │  Verification  │  │
│  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └──────┬─────────┘  │
│       │              │               │            │
│       └──────────────┼───────────────┘            │
│                      │ mpsc channels               │
│                      ▼                            │
│            ┌─────────────────┐                    │
│            │  Event Loop     │                    │
│            │  (frankentui)   │                    │
│            └───────┬─────────┘                    │
│                    │                              │
│  ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  Panel 1   │  Panel 2   │  Panel 3  │ P4  │   │
│  │ Benchmark  │ Recovery   │ Correct.  │ Sum │   │
│  └────────────┴────────────┴───────────┴─────┘   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Channel Messages
```rust
pub enum DashboardEvent {
    BenchmarkProgress { name: String, ops_per_sec: f64, elapsed: Duration },
    BenchmarkComplete { name: String, results: BenchmarkResults },
    CorruptionInjected { page: u32, pattern: String },
    RecoveryAttempt { group: u32, symbols_available: u32, needed: u32 },
    RecoverySuccess { page: u32, decode_proof: String },
    RecoveryFailure { page: u32, reason: String },
    CorrectnessCheck { workload: String, frank_hash: String, csqlite_hash: String, match_: bool },
    StatusMessage(String),
}
```

### frankentui Integration
- Review frankentui's widget system and layout primitives
- Use its app framework for event loop + terminal management
- Keyboard: Tab to switch panels, q to quit, r to run/restart
- Mouse support if frankentui provides it

### Headless Mode
When `--headless` flag is passed:
- Skip TUI initialization
- Still run all tests/benchmarks
- Output JSON results to stdout or file
- For CI environments without terminal

### Acceptance Criteria
- TUI binary compiles and launches
- Shows 4 panel layout (even if panels are placeholder text)
- Channel-based data feed works (send test events, verify display updates)
- Keyboard navigation between panels
- Headless mode outputs JSON
- Terminal resize handled gracefully

title: WASM Phase 6: Concurrent Writers in Browser — SharedArrayBuffer MVCC, Worker Pool

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# Phase 6: Concurrent Writers in Browser — The Killer Feature

## Goal
Enable FrankenSQLite's signature feature — page-level MVCC concurrent writers — in the browser via SharedArrayBuffer and Web Worker pool. This is what no other browser SQLite can do.

## Why This Matters
Every existing browser SQLite (sql.js, wa-sqlite, official sqlite-wasm) is single-writer. When one write transaction is in progress, all other writes must wait. FrankenSQLite's MVCC page-level versioning can change this — multiple Workers can write simultaneously as long as they touch different pages.

## Architecture
```
Worker Pool (4 Workers, each with FrankenSQLite WASM instance)
    |
    | SharedArrayBuffer (page lock table + version chains)
    |
    ├── Worker 1: INSERT INTO users ...   (page 47)
    ├── Worker 2: INSERT INTO orders ...  (page 112)
    ├── Worker 3: UPDATE stats ...        (page 5)
    └── Worker 4: SELECT ... (read-only, no conflict)
```

## SharedArrayBuffer Usage
- **Page lock table**: Atomics on SharedArrayBuffer for page-level locks
- **Version chain metadata**: Shared version counters for visibility decisions
- **Transaction IDs**: Atomic counter for TxnId generation

## Browser Requirements
- SharedArrayBuffer (Chrome 67+, Firefox 79+, Safari 15.2+)
- COOP/COEP headers (required for SAB in most browsers)
- Web Workers (universal)

## Limitations
- COOP/COEP headers break some third-party scripts (analytics, ads)
- Safari has limited SharedArrayBuffer support
- Falls back to single-writer mode when SAB is unavailable

## Phases Within Phase 6
1. SharedArrayBuffer page lock table
2. MVCC visibility via shared version counters
3. Worker pool with shared-memory coordination
4. Conflict detection and retry logic
5. Fallback to single-writer when SAB unavailable

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# 5C.4: Route SeekRowid/SeekGE/SeekLE/SeekGT/SeekLT through B-tree cursor

## What

Seek opcodes perform point lookups or range scans on B-trees. They're critical for WHERE
clause evaluation with indexes and for point queries by rowid.

## Opcodes

- **SeekRowid(cursor, jump_if_not_found, rowid_reg)**: Seek to exact rowid.
  → Maps to `BtCursor::table_move_to(rowid)` → SeekResult::Found or NotFound
- **SeekGE(cursor, jump_if_done, key_reg)**: Position at first row >= key.
  → Maps to `BtCursor::table_move_to(key)` then adjust if NotFound
- **SeekGT(cursor, jump_if_done, key_reg)**: Position at first row > key.
  → SeekGE then skip if exact match
- **SeekLE(cursor, jump_if_done, key_reg)**: Position at last row <= key.
  → table_move_to then prev() if beyond
- **SeekLT(cursor, jump_if_done, key_reg)**: Position at last row < key.
  → SeekLE then skip if exact match
- **NotExists(cursor, jump_if_not_found, rowid_reg)**: Like SeekRowid but different jump logic
- **Found/NotFound**: For index B-trees (key comparison, not rowid)

## Where to change

**Primary:** `crates/fsqlite-vdbe/src/engine.rs` — handlers for each seek opcode

## table_move_to semantics

BtCursor::table_move_to(rowid) performs binary search:
1. Start at root page
2. At interior pages: binary search cell keys to find child pointer
3. Descend to child
4. At leaf page: binary search cells for rowid
5. Return SeekResult::Found (cursor positioned on row) or SeekResult::NotFound (cursor
   positioned where row WOULD be, for range queries)

## Index seek (Found/NotFound/NoConflict)

For index B-trees, the key is a composite blob (not a simple rowid). The seek compares
using the record comparison function with collation awareness. These opcodes use
`BtCursor::move_to(key_blob)` instead of `table_move_to(rowid)`.

## Performance impact

Seek operations are the hot path for indexed queries:
- Point query: O(log N) page reads (B-tree height, typically 3-4 for millions of rows)
- Index range scan: O(log N) seek + O(K) sequential reads for K matching rows
- Full table scan fallback (no index): O(N) via Rewind+Next

Getting this right is essential for query performance.

## Tests

- `test_seek_rowid_found`: INSERT row, SeekRowid, verify Found
- `test_seek_rowid_not_found`: SeekRowid non-existent rowid, verify jump
- `test_seek_ge_range_scan`: INSERT 100 rows, SeekGE(50), Next loop → rows 50-100
- `test_seek_lt_range_scan`: INSERT 100 rows, SeekLT(50), Prev loop → rows 1-49
- `test_seek_on_empty_table`: All seek variants on empty table → appropriate jumps

title: §4.16 Observability: Task Inspector + Evidence Ledger + Diagnostics
description:
E2E Test:
- test_e2e_bd_3q1g_compliance: concrete E2E identifier for structure lint compliance.

Implement asupersync-native observability including Task Inspector API, Evidence Ledger with deterministic replay, and diagnostic repro bundles (§4.16 + §4.16.1, spec lines ~5118-5174).

SCOPE AND PURPOSE: FrankenSQLite MUST surface production and lab diagnostics following the "no vibes" philosophy — if something times out or aborts, the system must explain why with evidence. Three components: Task Inspector (live visibility), Evidence Ledger (bounded deterministic decision record), and Repro Bundles (artifact emission for deterministic reproduction).

KEY DATA STRUCTURES AND APIs:
- TaskInspector: blocked_reason(task_id), budget_usage(task_id), mask_depth(task_id), obligations(task_id), cancel_status(task_id) — structured explanations for why tasks are blocked or cancelled.
- EvidenceEntry: {decision_id: u64, kind: DecisionKind (Cancel/Race/Scheduler/Commit), context: DecisionContext {task_id, region_id, lane: Cancel|Timed|Ready}, candidates: Vec<Candidate {id, score, description}>, constraints: Vec<Constraint>, chosen: CandidateId, rationale: Vec<Reason>, witnesses: Vec<TraceEventId>}.
- EvidenceLedger: {ring: RingBuffer<EvidenceEntry>, emission_policy: Lab|Production, artifacts_dir: Option<PathBuf>}. record(entry), spill_to_artifacts(), entries().

EVENTS THAT MUST BE RECORDED: (1) Cancellation propagation: who cancelled whom, and why. (2) Race/timeout/hedge winner selection and loser drain proofs. (3) Scheduler choices under deadlines/budgets: lane + tie-break decisions. (4) Commit/abort decisions: FCW conflicts, SSI pivot aborts, merge eligibility, retry/merge policy decisions with contention telemetry.

COMMIT-LEDGER RULE (Normative): If a commit/abort decision is influenced by contention telemetry or policy inference, the ledger MUST include: regime_id/window, writers_active (or N), M2_hat/P_eff_hat (§18.4.1), f_merge/rung yields (§18.7), evaluated candidate actions with expected losses (§18.8).

DETERMINISM REQUIREMENTS: Field ordering MUST be deterministic. Candidate ordering: stable by (score desc, id asc). Witness references MUST be stable under replay (trace event IDs or hashes). Ledger size bounded: ring buffer in production, spill-to-artifacts in lab.

EMISSION POLICY:
- Lab: Evidence ledger MUST be emitted for any failing test, any SSI abort, any commit abort due to FCW/SSI/merge.
- Production: Sampleable and gated (PRAGMA or env). MUST NOT impose unbounded overhead or allocate on hot paths.

CONFIGURATION PARAMETERS: Ring buffer capacity. ASUPERSYNC_TEST_ARTIFACTS_DIR for lab artifact emission. PRAGMA or env for production sampling gate.

ERROR HANDLING: Production mode must not allocate on hot recording paths. Ring buffer overwrites oldest entries when full. Lab mode spills to artifacts directory on failure.

UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS (9 tests): (1) Deterministic field order: two entries with same data produce byte-identical serialization. (2) Candidate ordering stable (score desc, id asc) across serializations. (3) Ring buffer bounded: capacity 100, insert 150, only latest 100 retained. (4) Lab emission on SSI abort: entry with kind=Commit and SSI abort rationale. (5) Production no hot-path allocation: recording with sampling disabled triggers no heap allocation. (6) Repro bundle emitted on failure: artifacts dir contains repro manifest with trace artifacts. (7) Commit ledger includes contention state (regime_id, writers_active, candidate actions). (8) Task inspector blocked reason returns structured info. (9) Witness references stable under replay.

# §4.16 Observability: Task Inspector + Evidence Ledger + Diagnostics

## Spec Reference
COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md §4.16 + §4.16.1 (lines ~5118–5174)

## Scope

### Task Inspector API
FrankenSQLite MUST surface asupersync-native diagnostics for production and lab use:
- **Live visibility** into: blocked reasons, budget usage, mask depth, held obligations, and cancellation status.
- **Structured explanations** for cancellation propagation and blocked tasks (why are we stuck? who holds what?).
- This is a direct consequence of the "no vibes" philosophy: if something times out or aborts, the system must be able to explain why with evidence.

### Deterministic Repro Bundles
When `ASUPERSYNC_TEST_ARTIFACTS_DIR` is set in harness runs:
- Failures MUST emit a repro manifest and trace artifacts.
- These artifacts must recreate the schedule and cancellation points for deterministic reproduction.

### Evidence Ledger (§4.16.1 — Galaxy-Brain Explainability)
A bounded, deterministic record of *why* a cancellation/race/scheduler decision occurred (trace-backed, replay-stable).

#### Events That MUST Be Recorded
- **Cancellation propagation**: who cancelled whom, and why.
- **Race/timeout/hedge winner selection**: and loser drain proofs.
- **Scheduler choices under deadlines/budgets**: lane + tie-break decisions.
- **Commit/abort decisions**: FCW conflicts, SSI pivot aborts, merge eligibility, and any retry/merge policy decisions that depend on contention telemetry.

#### Commit-Ledger Rule (Normative)
If a commit/abort decision is influenced by contention telemetry or policy inference (rather than a pure correctness check), the ledger MUST include the contention state used, at minimum:
- `regime_id` / window identifier (if any)
- `writers_active` (or the `N` used in the model)
- `M2_hat` / `P_eff_hat` (if used; §18.4.1)
- `f_merge` / merge rung yields (if used; §18.7)
- Evaluated candidate actions with expected losses (§18.8)

#### Minimum Ledger Entry Schema (Normative)
```text
EvidenceEntry := {
  decision_id : u64,
  kind        : { cancel, race, scheduler, commit },
  context     : { task_id: u64, region_id: u64, lane: {Cancel, Timed, Ready} },
  candidates  : Vec<Candidate>,
  constraints : Vec<Constraint>,
  chosen      : CandidateId,
  rationale   : Vec<Reason>,
  witnesses   : Vec<TraceEventId>,
}
```

#### Determinism Requirements
- **Field ordering** MUST be deterministic.
- **Candidate ordering** MUST be deterministic (stable by `(score desc, id asc)`).
- **Witness references** MUST be stable under replay (trace event IDs or hashes).
- **Ledger size** MUST be bounded: ring buffer in production, spill-to-artifacts in lab mode.

#### Emission Policy (Required)
| Mode | Policy |
|---|---|
| **Lab** | Evidence ledger MUST be emitted for any failing test, any SSI abort, and any commit abort due to FCW/SSI/merge. |
| **Production** | Evidence ledger SHOULD be sampleable and gated (PRAGMA or env). It MUST NOT impose unbounded overhead or allocate on hot paths. |

## Implementation Guidance

### Core Types (in `crates/fsqlite-async/src/observability.rs` or similar)
```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct EvidenceEntry {
    pub decision_id: u64,
    pub kind: DecisionKind,
    pub context: DecisionContext,
    pub candidates: Vec<Candidate>,
    pub constraints: Vec<Constraint>,
    pub chosen: CandidateId,
    pub rationale: Vec<Reason>,
    pub witnesses: Vec<TraceEventId>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
pub enum DecisionKind { Cancel, Race, Scheduler, Commit }

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct DecisionContext {
    pub task_id: u64,
    pub region_id: u64,
    pub lane: Lane,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
pub enum Lane { Cancel, Timed, Ready }

pub type CandidateId = u64;
pub type TraceEventId = u64;

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct Candidate {
    pub id: CandidateId,
    pub score: f64,
    pub description: String,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct Constraint { pub description: String }
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct Reason { pub description: String }
```

### Task Inspector
```rust
pub struct TaskInspector { /* ... */ }

impl TaskInspector {
    /// Returns structured info about why a task is blocked
    pub fn blocked_reason(&self, task_id: u64) -> Option<BlockedReason>;
    /// Returns current budget usage for a task
    pub fn budget_usage(&self, task_id: u64) -> BudgetUsage;
    /// Returns mask depth for a task
    pub fn mask_depth(&self, task_id: u64) -> usize;
    /// Returns obligations held by a task
    pub fn obligations(&self, task_id: u64) -> Vec<ObligationInfo>;
    /// Returns cancellation status
    pub fn cancel_status(&self, task_id: u64) -> CancelStatus;
}
```

### Evidence Ledger
```rust
pub struct EvidenceLedger {
    ring: RingBuffer<EvidenceEntry>,
    emission_policy: EmissionPolicy,
    artifacts_dir: Option<PathBuf>,
}

pub enum EmissionPolicy {
    Lab,        // always emit on failure/abort
    Production, // sample-gated, no hot-path allocation
}

impl EvidenceLedger {
    pub fn record(&mut self, entry: EvidenceEntry);
    pub fn spill_to_artifacts(&self) -> io::Result<PathBuf>;
    pub fn entries(&self) -> &[EvidenceEntry];
}
```

### Ring Buffer + Artifact Spill
- In production: bounded ring buffer, oldest entries overwritten.
- In lab mode: ring buffer + spill to `ASUPERSYNC_TEST_ARTIFACTS_DIR` on failure.

## Unit Test Specifications

### Test 1: `test_evidence_entry_deterministic_field_order`
Create two `EvidenceEntry` values with the same data but constructed in different order. Serialize both. Assert byte-identical output (deterministic field ordering).

### Test 2: `test_candidate_ordering_stable`
Create an `EvidenceEntry` with candidates having various scores. Assert candidates are ordered by `(score desc, id asc)`. Verify this ordering is stable across multiple serializations.

### Test 3: `test_ring_buffer_bounded_size`
Create a ledger with ring buffer capacity 100. Insert 150 entries. Assert only the latest 100 are retained. Assert no unbounded memory growth.

### Test 4: `test_lab_emission_on_ssi_abort`
Configure emission policy as Lab. Trigger an SSI abort event. Assert the evidence ledger contains an entry with `kind=Commit` and rationale explaining the SSI abort.

### Test 5: `test_production_emission_no_hot_path_alloc`
Configure emission policy as Production with sampling disabled. Record an event. Assert no heap allocation occurred on the recording path (use a custom allocator or allocation counter).

### Test 6: `test_repro_bundle_emitted_on_failure`
Set `ASUPERSYNC_TEST_ARTIFACTS_DIR` to a temp directory. Trigger a test failure. Assert a repro manifest file exists in the artifacts directory containing trace artifacts sufficient for schedule replay.

### Test 7: `test_commit_ledger_includes_contention_state`
Record a commit decision influenced by contention telemetry. Assert the evidence entry includes `regime_id`, `writers_active`, and evaluated candidate actions with expected losses per the commit-ledger rule.

### Test 8: `test_task_inspector_blocked_reason`
Create a task inspector with a known blocked task. Query `blocked_reason(task_id)`. Assert the returned `BlockedReason` includes structured information about what the task is waiting on (obligation, lock, budget, etc.).

### Test 9: `test_witness_references_stable_under_replay`
Record evidence entries with witness references. Replay the same schedule. Assert witness `TraceEventId` values are identical across both runs.

title: §4.3.2 MVCC Invariant Monitors (INV-1 through INV-7 + INV-SSI-FP)
description:
Implement concrete e-process monitor definitions for all MVCC hard invariants INV-1 through INV-7 plus statistical invariant INV-SSI-FP (§4.3, spec lines ~4131-4247).

SCOPE AND PURPOSE: Define the create_mvcc_monitors() factory with per-invariant calibrated (p0, lambda, alpha) parameters reflecting qualitative violation characteristics. Each invariant has a distinct calibration tier — using identical parameters for all invariants is explicitly wrong per the alien-artifact calibration discipline.

KEY DATA STRUCTURES AND APIs:
- create_mvcc_monitors() -> Vec<EProcess>: Factory returning 7 monitors (INV-1 through INV-7) with correct per-invariant configs.
- observe_lock_exclusivity(lock_table, active_transactions) -> bool: INV-2 observation function that checks page->holders for duplicates, detects ghost locks (unknown txn), and cross-checks lock_table vs txn lock sets.
- ActiveTxnInfo: {state: TxnState, page_locks: Vec<PageNumber>} — per-transaction metadata for lock observation.

INVARIANT DEFINITIONS AND CALIBRATION:
- Catastrophic tier (INV-1 Monotonicity, INV-2 Lock Exclusivity, INV-7 Serialized Mode): p0=1e-9, lambda=0.999, alpha=1e-6, max_evalue=1e18. Violations imply hardware faults or fundamental logic errors. ~20 violations sufficient to reject.
- Moderate tier (INV-3 Version Chain Order, INV-4 Write Set Consistency, INV-5 Snapshot Stability, INV-6 Commit Atomicity): p0=1e-6, lambda=0.9, alpha=0.001, max_evalue=1e15.
- Statistical tier (INV-SSI-FP): p0 calibrated to expected FP baseline (~0.5-5%), NOT 0.001. This monitors drift beyond baseline, not hard violations.

ALGORITHMS:
- E-process update per observation: E_t = E_{t-1} * (1 + lambda * (X_t - p0)).
- Expected detection delay: N_detect ~ log(1/alpha) / KL(p1 || p0).
- INV-2 observation: build page_holders map from active txn lock sets, check for >1 holder per page, cross-check lock_table entries against txn state and lock sets.

CONFIGURATION PARAMETERS: Per-invariant (p0, lambda, alpha, max_evalue) as specified above. Power analysis formula provided for tuning.

ERROR HANDLING: Violation detected -> e-value jumps ~2x. Rejection produces proof certificate with monitor name, final e-value, threshold, observation count, and violation indices. Under null (100K obs, no violations), e-values stay <= 2.0.

UNIT TEST REQUIREMENTS (12 tests): (1) create_mvcc_monitors returns exactly 7 monitors with correct names. (2) INV-1 detects TxnId regression. (3) INV-2 no-violation scenario: 100 pages, each held by one txn. (4) INV-2 dual-holder detection. (5) INV-2 ghost lock detection (unknown txn). (6) INV-2 lock_table vs txn lock set disagreement. (7) Catastrophic invariants have strict config (p0<=1e-9, lambda>=0.999, alpha<=1e-6). (8) Moderate invariants share moderate config tier. (9) INV-SSI-FP with p0=0.05: no rejection at 4% rate, rejection at 15% rate within 500 obs. (10) Rejection includes proof certificate. (11) 100K obs under null: no false alarms across all 7 monitors. (12) Inactive txn holding lock detected by cross-check.

E2E TEST: Run representative workload under lab runtime, inject one violation per invariant class, verify monitors detect and emit evidence with deterministic reproduction seed.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: Per-invariant calibration correctly reflects violation severity. Observation functions detect all specified violation classes including ghost locks and cross-check failures. Factory produces correctly-named monitors. Proof certificates are complete and actionable.

Added tests: test_create_mvcc_monitors_returns_eight, INV-2 violation-class tests, calibration-tier tests, test_inv_ssi_fp_calibration_differs, and test_e2e_invariant_monitors_catch_injected_violations. # §4.3.2 MVCC Invariant Monitors (INV-1 through INV-7 + INV-SSI-FP)

**Spec Reference:** COMPREHENSIVE_SPEC_FOR_FRANKENSQLITE_V1.md §4.3, lines 4131–4247

## Overview

Implement the concrete e-process monitor definitions for all MVCC hard invariants
(INV-1 through INV-7) plus the statistical invariant INV-SSI-FP. Each monitor has
calibrated `(p0, lambda, alpha)` parameters reflecting the qualitative violation
characteristics of that invariant. This is the `create_mvcc_monitors()` factory
and associated observation functions.

## Calibration Discipline (Alien-Artifact)

**CRITICAL:** Using identical `(p0, lambda, alpha)` for all invariants is WRONG.
Each invariant has qualitatively different violation characteristics:

- **INV-1 (monotonicity):** Enforced by `AtomicU64::fetch_add`. A violation implies
  a hardware fault. `p0` should be ~1e-9 to 1e-15.
- **INV-SSI-FP (false positive rate):** Has an EXPECTED baseline of ~0.5–5%.
  `p0 = 0.001` would trigger false alarms constantly.

Per-invariant power analysis: for a monitor with `p0` and `lambda`, the expected
detection delay (observations to reject H0) when the true violation rate is `p1` is:

```
N_detect ≈ log(1/alpha) / KL(p1 || p0)
```

## Invariant Definitions and Monitor Configs

### INV-1: TxnId/CommitSeq Monotonicity
- **What:** `TxnId` (begin IDs) and `CommitSeq` (commit clock) are strictly increasing
- **Enforcement:** Hardware atomics (`AtomicU64::fetch_add`)
- **Violation class:** Catastrophic (hardware fault or fundamental logic error)
- **Config:** `p0: 1e-9, lambda: 0.999, alpha: 1e-6, max_evalue: 1e18`
- **Response:** Fail-fast on first observed violation (assert/panic). E-process
  provides an auditable, anytime-valid ledger for long-running fuzz/lab traces.

### INV-2: Lock Exclusivity
- **What:** No two active transactions hold the same page lock
- **Enforcement:** CAS operations on lock table
- **Violation class:** Catastrophic (logic bug in lock management)
- **Config:** `p0: 1e-9, lambda: 0.999, alpha: 1e-6, max_evalue: 1e18`

#### INV-2 Observation Function (from spec):

```rust
struct ActiveTxnInfo {
    state: TxnState,
    page_locks: Vec<PageNumber>,
}

fn observe_lock_exclusivity(
    lock_table: &InProcessPageLockTable,
    active_transactions: &HashMap<TxnId, ActiveTxnInfo>,
) -> bool {
    // Build page -> holders map from per-transaction lock sets
    let mut page_holders: HashMap<PageNumber, Vec<TxnId>> = HashMap::new();
    for (txn_id, txn) in active_transactions {
        if txn.state == TxnState::Active {
            for &pgno in &txn.page_locks {
                page_holders.entry(pgno).or_default().push(*txn_id);
            }
        }
    }
    // Check: any page with >1 holder is a violation
    for (pgno, holders) in &page_holders {
        if holders.len() > 1 {
            return true; // VIOLATION
        }
    }
    // Cross-check: every lock_table entry must be present in the txn's lock set
    // (no "ghost" or leaked locks)
    for (&pgno, &holder) in lock_table.iter() {
        let Some(txn) = active_transactions.get(&holder) else {
            return true; // VIOLATION (lock held by unknown txn)
        };
        if txn.state != TxnState::Active || !txn.page_locks.contains(&pgno) {
            return true; // VIOLATION (lock_table and txn lock set disagree)
        }
    }
    false // no violation
}
```

**Detection behavior for INV-2 (from spec):** With `lambda=0.999, p0=1e-9, alpha=1e-6`,
threshold is `1/alpha = 1,000,000`. Each violation approximately doubles the e-value
(`1 + lambda * (1 - p0) ≈ 2.0`). ~20 violations (`log2(10^6) ≈ 20`) are sufficient
to cross the threshold, even intermixed with millions of non-violations.

### INV-3: Version Chain Order
- **What:** Versions are ordered by descending `CommitSeq`
- **Enforcement:** Correct insert ordering in version chain
- **Violation class:** Subtle (wrong version served to reader)
- **Config:** `p0: 1e-6, lambda: 0.9, alpha: 0.001, max_evalue: 1e15`

### INV-4: Write Set Consistency
- **What:** Write set only contains locked pages
- **Enforcement:** Lock-before-write invariant
- **Violation class:** Moderate (data corruption risk)
- **Config:** `p0: 1e-6, lambda: 0.9, alpha: 0.001, max_evalue: 1e15`

### INV-5: Snapshot Stability
- **What:** A transaction's snapshot (`high` field) is immutable after capture
- **Enforcement:** Read-set immutability during transaction lifetime
- **Violation class:** Moderate (phantom reads, stale data)
- **Config:** `p0: 1e-6, lambda: 0.9, alpha: 0.001, max_evalue: 1e15`

### INV-6: Commit Atomicity
- **What:** Committed transaction's pages all become visible atomically
- **Enforcement:** All-or-nothing page visibility on commit
- **Violation class:** Moderate (partial commit visible = data corruption)
- **Config:** `p0: 1e-6, lambda: 0.9, alpha: 0.001, max_evalue: 1e15`

### INV-7: Serialized Mode Exclusivity
- **What:** At most one serialized writer active at any time
- **Enforcement:** Global mutex correctness
- **Violation class:** Catastrophic (serialized mode is a safety fallback)
- **Config:** `p0: 1e-9, lambda: 0.999, alpha: 1e-6, max_evalue: 1e18`

### INV-SSI-FP: SSI False Positive Rate (Statistical)
- **What:** SSI conflict detection false positive rate stays within expected bounds
- **Violation class:** Statistical (degraded performance, not correctness)
- **Config:** Must have `p0` calibrated to expected FP baseline (~0.5–5%), NOT 0.001
- **Note:** This is a *statistical* invariant, not a hard invariant. The e-process
  monitors whether the FP rate has drifted beyond the calibrated baseline.

## Factory Function

```rust
fn create_mvcc_monitors() -> Vec<EProcess> {
    vec![
        EProcess::new("INV-1: TxnId/CommitSeq Monotonicity", EProcessConfig {
            p0: 1e-9, lambda: 0.999, alpha: 1e-6, max_evalue: 1e18,
        }),
        EProcess::new("INV-2: Lock Exclusivity", EProcessConfig {
            p0: 1e-9, lambda: 0.999, alpha: 1e-6, max_evalue: 1e18,
        }),
        EProcess::new("INV-3: Version Chain Order", EProcessConfig {
            p0: 1e-6, lambda: 0.9, alpha: 0.001, max_evalue: 1e15,
        }),
        EProcess::new("INV-4: Write Set Consistency", EProcessConfig {
            p0: 1e-6, lambda: 0.9, alpha: 0.001, max_evalue: 1e15,
        }),
        EProcess::new("INV-5: Snapshot Stability", EProcessConfig {
            p0: 1e-6, lambda: 0.9, alpha: 0.001, max_evalue: 1e15,
        }),
        EProcess::new("INV-6: Commit Atomicity", EProcessConfig {
            p0: 1e-6, lambda: 0.9, alpha: 0.001, max_evalue: 1e15,
        }),
        EProcess::new("INV-7: Serialized Mode Exclusivity", EProcessConfig {
            p0: 1e-9, lambda: 0.999, alpha: 1e-6, max_evalue: 1e18,
        }),
    ]
}
```

## Usage Pattern (from spec)

```rust
// In the test loop, after each operation:
let violated = observe_lock_exclusivity(&lock_table, &active_transactions);
inv2_eprocess.observe(violated);
if inv2_eprocess.rejected {
    panic!(
        "INV-2 violated: e-value {} >= threshold {} after {} observations",
        inv2_eprocess.e_value(),
        inv2_eprocess.config.threshold(),
        inv2_eprocess.observations,
    );
}
```

After 1000 operations with no violations, `E_1000 ~ 1.0` (fluctuates around 1 due to
the martingale property).

## Proof Certificate

If an e-process detects a violation, it provides a **proof certificate** that the
invariant was violated, including the exact sequence of operations that caused it.
This is not a test that passes or fails — it's a continuously running formal monitor.

## Unit Test Specifications

### Test 1: `test_create_mvcc_monitors_returns_seven`
Call `create_mvcc_monitors()`. Assert it returns exactly 7 monitors with the
correct names matching "INV-1" through "INV-7".

### Test 2: `test_inv1_monotonicity_detects_regression`
Create INV-1 monitor. Feed observations where `TxnId` is compared against previous.
Inject a single regression (current < previous). Assert e-value jumps by ~2.0x.

### Test 3: `test_inv2_lock_exclusivity_no_violation`
Set up a lock table with 100 pages, each held by exactly one transaction.
Call `observe_lock_exclusivity()`. Assert returns `false`.

### Test 4: `test_inv2_lock_exclusivity_dual_holder`
Set up a lock table where page 42 is claimed by two different active transactions.
Call `observe_lock_exclusivity()`. Assert returns `true`.

### Test 5: `test_inv2_ghost_lock_detection`
Set up a lock table entry pointing to a `TxnId` that is not in the active
transactions map. Call `observe_lock_exclusivity()`. Assert returns `true`
(ghost lock detected).

### Test 6: `test_inv2_lock_table_txn_disagreement`
Set up a lock table entry for page P held by txn T, but txn T's `page_locks`
does not include P. Call `observe_lock_exclusivity()`. Assert returns `true`.

### Test 7: `test_catastrophic_invariants_have_strict_config`
For INV-1, INV-2, INV-7 (catastrophic class): assert `p0 <= 1e-9`,
`lambda >= 0.999`, `alpha <= 1e-6`. These must be the strictest configs.

### Test 8: `test_moderate_invariants_have_moderate_config`
For INV-3, INV-4, INV-5, INV-6 (moderate class): assert `p0 == 1e-6`,
`lambda == 0.9`, `alpha == 0.001`. These share a moderate config tier.

### Test 9: `test_inv_ssi_fp_calibration_differs`
Create an INV-SSI-FP monitor with `p0 = 0.05` (5% expected baseline).
Feed observations at rate 0.04 (below baseline) for 10,000 steps.
Assert no rejection. Then feed at rate 0.15 (3x baseline). Assert rejection
within 500 observations.

### Test 10: `test_monitor_rejection_includes_proof_certificate`
Run INV-3 monitor and inject 50 violations. Upon rejection, assert the
proof certificate contains: monitor name, final e-value, threshold, observation
count, and the observation indices where violations occurred.

### Test 11: `test_eprocess_under_null_no_false_alarm`
Run all 7 MVCC monitors for 100,000 observations each with zero violations.
Assert none reject (e-values should all be <= 2.0, well below thresholds).

### Test 12: `test_cross_check_lock_table_consistency`
Set up a scenario where `lock_table` has an entry for page P -> txn T, but
txn T has `state == TxnState::Committed` (not Active). Assert
`observe_lock_exclusivity()` returns `true` (inactive txn holding lock).

# Task 4.1: @frankensqlite/sdk Package Scaffolding

## What
Create the TypeScript package structure that wraps the WASM core with an ergonomic developer API.

## Package Structure
```
packages/sdk/
├── package.json
├── tsconfig.json
├── tsconfig.build.json
├── vitest.config.ts
├── src/
│   ├── index.ts              # Public exports
│   ├── database.ts           # FrankenDB class
│   ├── statement.ts          # PreparedStatement
│   ├── transaction.ts        # Transaction support
│   ├── worker-client.ts      # Worker RPC client (Comlink)
│   ├── types.ts              # TypeScript type definitions
│   ├── errors.ts             # FrankenSQLiteError class
│   └── utils.ts              # Helpers
├── tests/
│   ├── database.test.ts
│   ├── statement.test.ts
│   └── transaction.test.ts
└── README.md
```

## Build Configuration
- TypeScript 5.x with strict mode
- ES2022 target (modern browsers only)
- ES module output with .d.ts declarations
- vitest for testing (supports browser testing)
- tsup or rollup for bundling

## package.json
```json
{
  "name": "@frankensqlite/sdk",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "type": "module",
  "main": "dist/index.mjs",
  "types": "dist/index.d.ts",
  "exports": {
    ".": { "import": "./dist/index.mjs", "types": "./dist/index.d.ts" },
    "./worker": { "import": "./dist/worker.mjs" }
  },
  "peerDependencies": {
    "@frankensqlite/core": "^0.1.0"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "comlink": "^4.4"
  }
}
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- Package builds successfully with `npm run build`
- TypeScript strict mode passes
- Tests run with vitest
- Types correctly exported

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Benchmark Fairness Protocol: Identical PRAGMAs, Page Size, Cache Normalization

### Why This Is Critical
Benchmarking FrankenSQLite vs C SQLite is meaningless if they're running with different settings. A 10x speedup that's actually caused by different `synchronous` mode is worthless. Both backends MUST use identical configuration.

### Standard Benchmark Settings
```sql
-- Applied to BOTH backends before any benchmark
PRAGMA page_size = 4096;           -- Standard SQLite page size
PRAGMA cache_size = -64000;        -- 64MB page cache (negative = KB)
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;         -- WAL mode (FrankenSQLite's natural mode)
PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;       -- Balance between durability and speed
PRAGMA temp_store = MEMORY;        -- Temp tables in memory
PRAGMA mmap_size = 0;              -- Disable mmap (isolate our page cache behavior)
PRAGMA auto_vacuum = NONE;         -- No auto-vacuum (avoid background I/O)
PRAGMA locking_mode = NORMAL;      -- Standard locking
```

### Why Each Setting
| PRAGMA | Value | Rationale |
|--------|-------|-----------|
| page_size | 4096 | Default SQLite page size, most common in production |
| cache_size | -64000 | Large enough to fit test databases in cache |
| journal_mode | WAL | FrankenSQLite's natural mode; also C SQLite's fastest concurrent mode |
| synchronous | NORMAL | Production-realistic; FULL is too slow, OFF is unrealistic |
| temp_store | MEMORY | Avoid disk I/O variance from temp files |
| mmap_size | 0 | Ensure we're testing our page cache, not the OS |
| auto_vacuum | NONE | Eliminate non-deterministic background vacuuming |

### Fairness Verification
Before each benchmark run:
```rust
fn verify_pragma_settings(conn: &dyn SqlBackend) -> Result<()> {
    let settings = [
        ("page_size", "4096"),
        ("cache_size", "-64000"),
        ("journal_mode", "wal"),
        ("synchronous", "1"),  // NORMAL = 1
        ("temp_store", "2"),   // MEMORY = 2
        ("mmap_size", "0"),
        ("auto_vacuum", "0"),  // NONE = 0
    ];
    for (pragma, expected) in settings {
        let actual = conn.query(&format!("PRAGMA {pragma}"))?;
        assert_eq!(actual, expected, "PRAGMA {pragma} mismatch");
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

### System-Level Controls
Beyond PRAGMAs, system factors affect benchmark fairness:
- **CPU frequency**: Use `cpupower frequency-set --governor performance` if available
- **Warmup**: Run each benchmark once before measuring (eliminate JIT/cache effects)
- **Multiple iterations**: Criterion handles this with statistical rigor
- **Fresh database copy**: Each benchmark iteration starts from a clean golden copy
- **Process isolation**: No other benchmarks running concurrently

### Documentation
Each benchmark report MUST include:
1. All PRAGMA settings used
2. System info: CPU model, RAM, disk type, OS
3. Rust toolchain version
4. Criterion configuration (sample_size, measurement_time)

### Tests
1. `test_pragma_verification_passes` — correct settings → no error
2. `test_pragma_verification_fails` — wrong setting → clear error
3. `test_pragma_applied_to_both_backends` — both FrankenSQLite and rusqlite get same settings
4. `test_wal_mode_active` — WAL mode confirmed active after setting
5. `test_cache_size_effective` — cache size is actually used (not ignored)

### Cross-Reference
- Related to bd-1w6k.6.1 (benchmark methodology) — this bead provides the detailed implementation.

### Acceptance Criteria
- All PRAGMAs applied and verified before every benchmark
- Verification function reusable across all benchmark scenarios
- 5 unit tests for the fairness module
- Benchmark reports include all settings
- No benchmark can run without passing fairness verification

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
# Task 1.5: Gate OS-Specific Deps in fsqlite-pager and fsqlite-wal

## What
Gate `parking_lot` and file I/O dependencies in the pager and WAL crates for wasm32 compilation.

## fsqlite-pager
- Uses `parking_lot::Mutex` for page cache synchronization
- Uses `std::fs` for rollback journal I/O
- ARC eviction uses crossbeam for concurrent eviction thread
- For wasm32: single-threaded page cache (RefCell), no rollback journal (in-memory only initially), no concurrent eviction

## fsqlite-wal
- Uses file I/O for WAL file append/read
- Uses checksums (crc32c) — these work on wasm32
- WAL index uses shared memory — gate for wasm32
- For wasm32: WAL is optional. In-memory databases don't need WAL. OPFS-backed databases may use a simplified WAL.

## Changes
1. Gate `parking_lot` → polyfill Mutex/RwLock from task 1.2
2. Gate file I/O paths behind `cfg(not(wasm32))`
3. Keep page cache logic (it's useful even in-memory)
4. WAL: provide no-op or in-memory WAL for wasm32 initially

## Acceptance Criteria
- Both crates compile to wasm32 with `--no-default-features --features wasm`
- Native tests unaffected

comments.text:
## CORRECTIONS (found during deep audit, 2026-03-02)

### Issue 1: asupersync in fsqlite-wal is a HARD dependency — MUST be made optional
The wal Cargo.toml has `asupersync = { workspace = true }` as a NON-OPTIONAL dependency. asupersync uses io_uring (Linux kernel API) and will absolutely NOT compile on wasm32. This must be changed to:
```toml
[target.'cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))'.dependencies]
asupersync = { workspace = true }
```
Files using asupersync in wal:
- `src/native_commit.rs` (async I/O for WAL writes)
- `src/group_commit.rs` (batched async writes)
- `src/wal_fec.rs` (FEC coding)
- `src/per_core_buffer.rs`
All of these must be gated behind `#[cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))]`.

### Issue 2: std::time::Instant is used in MULTIPLE wal source files
Found in: per_core_buffer.rs:5, native_commit.rs:24, wal_fec.rs:19, group_commit.rs:39, checkpoint_executor.rs:89
These all need the time polyfill or cfg gating.

### Issue 3: parking_lot listed but may be unused in wal source
`parking_lot = { workspace = true }` is listed in fsqlite-wal/Cargo.toml but no `use parking_lot` found in src/. Should verify and either gate or remove.

### Issue 4: Incorrect claim about pager crossbeam
The original comment says "ARC eviction uses crossbeam for concurrent eviction thread" — this is WRONG. fsqlite-pager/Cargo.toml has NO crossbeam dependency. The pager uses parking_lot::Condvar for arc_cache.rs synchronization, not crossbeam.

### Issue 5: Condvar polyfill needed
fsqlite-pager/src/arc_cache.rs:28 uses `parking_lot::{Condvar, Mutex}`. The sync polyfill from task 1.2 only covers Mutex, RwLock, Once, OnceCell — NOT Condvar. Either:
- Add Condvar to the polyfill (on wasm32, Condvar is a no-op since there's only one thread)
- Gate the arc_cache concurrent eviction path behind cfg(not(wasm32))

### Corrected pager changes
1. Replace `parking_lot::Mutex` → polyfill Mutex (page_buf.rs, arc_cache.rs)
2. Gate `parking_lot::Condvar` usage in arc_cache.rs (no wasm32 equivalent needed — single thread)
3. Make parking_lot conditional in Cargo.toml
4. Gate asupersync in dev-dependencies if present
5. Handle std::time::Duration in page_cache.rs:512 (test context, probably OK)
6. Handle std::time::Instant in s3_fifo.rs:1977

### Corrected wal changes

2. Gate all files that use asupersync (native_commit.rs, group_commit.rs, wal_fec.rs, per_core_buffer.rs)
3. Gate or replace all std::time::Instant usage
4. Verify parking_lot usage and gate if needed

comments.text:
## Task: Benchmark — concurrent write throughput (2/4/8/16 threads)

### What
THE benchmark that demonstrates FrankenSQLite's MVCC advantage. Multiple writer threads inserting concurrently. C SQLite serializes writers via WAL_WRITE_LOCK; FrankenSQLite's MVCC allows true parallel writes.

### Benchmark Design
- Each thread: INSERT 1000 rows into its own ID range
- Thread counts: 2, 4, 8, 16
- Measure: total wall-clock time, derive aggregate rows/sec
- All threads start simultaneously via barrier

### C SQLite Behavior (Expected)
- 1 writer at a time (WAL_WRITE_LOCK serialization)
- Other writers get SQLITE_BUSY, retry with exponential backoff
- Throughput roughly constant regardless of thread count (maybe slightly worse due to contention overhead)

### FrankenSQLite Behavior (Expected)
- Multiple writers proceed simultaneously (MVCC page-level versioning)
- No SQLITE_BUSY errors
- Throughput scales with thread count (up to I/O saturation)

### Key Metric: Scalability Factor
```
scalability = throughput(N_threads) / throughput(1_thread)
```
- C SQLite: scalability ≈ 1.0 (flat — serialized)
- FrankenSQLite: scalability > 1.0, ideally near N (linear scaling)

### Contention Variants
1. **No contention**: Each thread writes to its own table
2. **Shared table, non-overlapping keys**: Same table, different ID ranges
3. **Shared table, overlapping keys**: Same table, same key range (conflict-heavy)

### Acceptance Criteria
- Criterion benchmarks for all thread counts (2, 4, 8, 16)
- At least 2 contention variants
- Results clearly show scalability difference
- SQLITE_BUSY retry count tracked for C SQLite
- JSON output for TUI dashboard

title: P1: Wire RaptorQ self-healing to asupersync pipeline for production use
description:
## Problem

RaptorQ self-healing infrastructure is implemented (raptorq_integration.rs 2032 lines, repair_engine.rs, repair_symbols.rs, db_fec.rs, wal_fec.rs) but is not wired to the production WAL write/read path. The codec traits (PageSymbolSink, PageSymbolSource, SymbolCodec) and metrics (RaptorQMetrics, GLOBAL_RAPTORQ_METRICS) are defined but the encode/decode flow is disconnected.

## Why This Matters

MCP Agent Mail runs on machines with 8+ concurrent coding agents generating sustained write load. WAL corruption from power loss or disk errors would be catastrophic without self-healing. RaptorQ erasure coding provides:
- Encode repair symbols alongside data pages in WAL
- On corruption detection, decode original pages from surviving symbols
- No manual intervention or backup restoration

## Dependencies: NONE

RaptorQ operates at the byte/page level — it has nothing to do with SQL triggers, FTS5, or any SQL-level feature. It encodes raw page data.

## Implementation Plan

### 1. Implement concrete SymbolCodec using raptorq crate
Wire raptorq::Encoder::new() and raptorq::Decoder::decode() to the SymbolCodec trait methods. Configure:
- symbol_size from PipelineConfig (default: page_size, typically 4096)
- repair_overhead from PipelineConfig (default: 1.2x, meaning 20% overhead)
- max_source_symbols based on WAL segment size

### 2. Wire PageSymbolSink into WAL write path
After writing a data page to WAL:
1. Feed page bytes to RaptorQ encoder
2. Generate repair symbols
3. Append repair symbols to ECS (Erasure Code Store) adjacent to WAL
4. Record encode metrics via GLOBAL_RAPTORQ_METRICS

### 3. Wire PageSymbolSource into corruption recovery
On page read failure or checksum mismatch:
1. Detect corruption via page checksum validation
2. Collect available symbols from ECS for the affected page
3. Feed to RaptorQ decoder
4. Verify decoded page checksum
5. Write repaired page back to database file
6. Record repair metrics

### 4. Checkpoint-aware symbol lifecycle
- Repair symbols for checkpointed pages can be reclaimed
- Track WAL checkpoint progress
- Garbage collect expired symbols periodically

### 5. Configuration wiring
- FSQLITE_RAPTORQ_ENABLED (bool, default: false) — master enable
- FSQLITE_RAPTORQ_OVERHEAD (f32, default: 1.2) — repair symbol ratio
- FSQLITE_RAPTORQ_SEGMENT_SIZE (usize, default: 64) — pages per repair group

## Key Files
- crates/fsqlite-core/src/raptorq_integration.rs — trait definitions, pipeline config
- crates/fsqlite-core/src/repair_engine.rs — repair orchestration
- crates/fsqlite-core/src/repair_symbols.rs — symbol storage/retrieval
- crates/fsqlite-core/src/db_fec.rs — database-level FEC integration
- crates/fsqlite-core/src/wal_fec.rs — WAL-level FEC integration
- crates/fsqlite-core/src/wal.rs — WAL write path (sink integration point)

## Test Plan

### Unit Tests (20+ tests)

**Encode/decode correctness (6 tests):**
1. Single page encode → decode round-trip (4096 bytes)
2. Multi-page encode → decode (64 pages)
3. Encode with 20% overhead → survive 15% symbol loss
4. Encode with 50% overhead → survive 40% symbol loss
5. Decode with insufficient symbols → returns error (not garbage)
6. Empty page (all zeros) encode → decode correctness

**Corruption detection and repair (6 tests):**
7. Flip 1 bit in page → checksum detects → repair succeeds
8. Flip 10% of bytes → repair succeeds with sufficient symbols
9. Corrupt beyond repair threshold → returns unrecoverable error with diagnostics
10. Corrupt multiple non-adjacent pages → each repaired independently
11. Corrupt page header specifically → repair restores header
12. Repair with exact minimum symbols → succeeds at boundary

**WAL integration (4 tests):**
13. Write page to WAL → ECS symbols generated
14. Checkpoint → ECS symbols for checkpointed pages reclaimed
15. WAL wraparound → symbols cycle correctly
16. Write under BEGIN CONCURRENT → per-transaction symbol isolation

**Metrics (4 tests):**
17. encode_count increments on each write
18. decode_success_count increments on successful repair
19. decode_failure_count increments on unrecoverable corruption
20. overhead_bytes_total tracks ECS storage usage
21. repair_latency_ms histogram populated

**Config and lifecycle (3 tests):**
22. FSQLITE_RAPTORQ_ENABLED=false → no symbols generated, no overhead
23. Enable mid-session → symbols generated for new writes only
24. Segment size config affects repair group boundaries

### E2E Test Script: tests/e2e/test_raptorq_self_healing.sh
```
Tests: 30 assertions, 8 cases
Logging: JSONL structured output with per-assertion timing, corruption details, repair evidence
Cases:
  1. Normal write/read cycle with RaptorQ enabled — no repair needed
  2. Single page corruption (bit flip) — automatic repair, data integrity verified
  3. Multi-page corruption (5% random) — all repaired, query results unchanged
  4. Corruption beyond threshold (25%) — graceful error, no silent data loss
  5. Checkpoint reclamation — ECS shrinks after checkpoint
  6. Concurrent writers + corruption — isolation maintained during repair
  7. Performance: write latency with/without RaptorQ (must be <5% overhead)
  8. Cold start with corrupted DB — repair on first read
```

Each case logs:
```json
{"case": 2, "assertion": "repair_succeeded", "corruption_type": "bit_flip", "page": 42, "symbols_available": 80, "symbols_needed": 64, "repair_ms": 3, "status": "PASS"}
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- RaptorQ encode/decode functional on WAL write/read path
- Automatic corruption recovery in E2E test (5% random page corruption)
- Write latency overhead <5% (async symbol generation)
- FSQLITE_RAPTORQ_ENABLED=true activates the pipeline
- Graceful degradation when corruption exceeds repair capacity
- All 24 unit tests pass
- E2E test script passes with 30 assertions
- Metrics accurate and observable

comments.text:
## §7.7 PRAGMA integrity_check Implementation (5 Levels)

**Level 1 — Page-level:** Read every page. For B-tree pages: verify type flag valid (0x02, 0x05, 0x0A, 0x0D), verify header fields in range. Overflow, freelist trunk/leaf, lock-byte, and pointer map pages have different structures — MUST NOT be checked against B-tree type flags. If page checksums enabled, verify XXH3 for all page types.

**Level 2 — B-tree structural:** Cell pointers within bounds and non-overlapping. Cell content within cell content area. Interior child pointers reference valid pages. Keys sorted within each page. Keys in child subtrees bounded by parent keys. Freeblock list well-formed (no cycles). Fragmented byte count matches actual fragmentation.

**Level 3 — Record format:** Header varints valid. Serial types not 10 or 11 (reserved). Payload sizes match serial type declarations. Overflow chains well-formed.

**Level 4 — Cross-reference:** Every page accounted for (B-tree, freelist, or pointer-map). No page in multiple B-trees. Freelist structure consistent. Pointer map entries match actual parents (auto-vacuum mode).

**Level 5 — Schema:** sqlite_master readable. All entries parseable. Root page numbers match existing B-trees. For each index, verify entries match table data.

**Output:** List of error strings, or single string "ok" if no issues. Matches C SQLite behavior exactly.

## §7.8 Error Recovery by Checksum Type

**WAL frame checksum mismatch:** Frame at or beyond valid WAL end under cumulative rule (S7.5). Normal recovery truncates at first mismatch. FrankenSQLite MUST attempt repair first if matching .wal-fec group exists: locate WalFecGroupMeta, validate source frames using source_page_xxh3_128 (random-access, independent of broken chain), combine surviving sources + repair symbols, decode if >= K. If repair succeeds: treat as committed, checkpoint + reset WAL (persist repair). If repair fails: truncate WAL before damaged group (txn lost).

**XXH3 internal mismatch (buffer pool):** Return SQLITE_CORRUPT. Log page number, expected/actual hash. Evict from cache. Retry from WAL if page exists there. Otherwise corruption is persistent.

**CRC-32C mismatch (RaptorQ symbol):** Exclude corrupted symbol from decoding set. If |surviving| >= K total symbols (source + repair combined), decoding proceeds. Otherwise commit group unrecoverable.

**Database file corruption (integrity_check):** Reported as diagnostic text. WAL version supersedes corrupt page if available. Otherwise corruption permanent without backups.

SECTION 5 OF COMPREHENSIVE SPEC — MVCC FORMAL MODEL (REVISED)

This epic captures the *formal* MVCC model that FrankenSQLite must implement (single-process and multi-process), including the invariants, cross-process shared-memory coordination, SSI evidence/witness plane, commit sequencing, and the safe merge/rebase ladder.

If §3 (RaptorQ) is the information-theoretic durability substrate and §4 (asupersync) is the runtime/capability substrate, §5 is the *correctness substrate*: the model that makes the rest implementable without interpretive gaps.

SPEC REFERENCE: §5 (MVCC Formal Model (Revised))

KEY DEPENDENCIES:
- §3 (`bd-1hi`): RaptorQ-coded witness plane + patch/history compression + any "repairable" MVCC artifacts.
- §4 (`bd-3go`): `Cx`, Lab runtime, DPOR/interleaving tools, evidence ledger, cancellation/masking semantics.
- §2 (`bd-iwu`): why page-level MVCC, isolation semantics target, and boundary between layers.
- Related specs that must line up with §5 semantics: checksums/integrity (§7), buffer pool (§6), testing strategy (§17), probabilistic conflict model (§18), implementation phases (§16).

MAJOR SUBSECTIONS (ACTIONABLE OUTLINE; IMPLEMENTATION MUST FOLLOW):
- §5.1 Core Types: TxnId/CommitSeq/Snapshot/SchemaEpoch, PageVersion, VersionArena (no pointer chasing), page lock tables.
- §5.2–§5.3 MVCC Invariants + Visibility Predicate: what "visible" means and what must *never* happen.
- §5.4 Transaction Lifecycle: BEGIN/DEFERRED snapshot establishment, Read/Write, Commit/Abort state machine.
- §5.5 Safety Proofs (Theorems 1–6): translate proof obligations into runnable invariants + tests.
- §5.6 Cross-Process Coordination:
  - §5.6.1 SharedMemoryLayout
  - §5.6.2 TxnSlot (per-txn shared state) + crash recovery
  - §5.6.3 SharedPageLockTable (exclusive page locks) + rolling rebuild protocol
  - §5.6.4 SSI witness plane (RaptorQ-native evidence; no false negatives)
  - §5.6.5 GC coordination (horizon, scheduling, incremental pruning)
  - §5.6.6–§5.6.7 Compatibility mode + hybrid SHM protocol / legacy interop
- §5.7 Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI): witness objects, commit-time validation, refinement policy, abort/victim selection.
- §5.8 Conflict Detection & Resolution: first-committer-wins baseline + conflict responses; serialized/concurrent mutual exclusion.
- §5.9 Write Coordinator: native sequencer + compatibility WAL path; IPC transport + wire payload schemas; group commit batching.
- §5.10 Merge/Rebase Ladder:
  - §5.10.1 Intent logs (semantic ops + footprints)
  - §5.10.2 Deterministic rebase & index regeneration
  - §5.10.3 Structured page patch merges (parse/merge/repack; no raw XOR on SQLite pages)
  - §5.10.4 Commit-time merge policy (strict safety ladder)
  - §5.10.5 Proof obligations
  - §5.10.6–§5.10.8 History compression + commutativity/normal forms + merge certificates

TESTING MODEL (NON-NEGOTIABLE):
- Unit tests: invariants and edge cases at the type/module layer (visibility predicate, lock table semantics, TxnSlot crash recovery, GC horizon math, merge certificate verification).
- Property tests: proptest for MVCC invariants, merge algebra laws, determinism (same inputs -> same replay outcome), and structured page patch safety (parse/merge/repack soundness).
- Deterministic concurrency E2E: LabRuntime + systematic cancellation + DPOR/interleaving exploration for key races.
- Crash-consistency E2E: injected crashes at every durability boundary (WAL fsync, SHM update, marker append, witness publication).
- Logging/tracing: structured `tracing` spans and evidence artifacts sufficient to reproduce any failure without dumping full page buffers.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- [ ] All child beads of `bd-3t3` are closed, and the integrated MVCC subsystem passes workspace tests.
- [ ] The MVCC visibility predicate and invariants are encoded as runnable checks (debug assertions + invariant monitors where specified) and are exercised in both unit and property tests.
- [ ] Cross-process shared-memory coordination works under injected faults and supports restart recovery for TxnSlots/lock tables.
- [ ] SSI validation produces no false negatives (soundness), and abort policies are test-driven with deterministic scenarios.
- [ ] Merge/rebase paths are protected by merge certificates and verification; unsafe merges are rejected and logged with evidence.

## Success Criteria
- [ ] The MVCC model and invariants are explicit enough that we can implement without interpretive gaps (types, state machines, safety rules).
- [ ] Concurrency semantics are validated by deterministic lab tests (not just ad-hoc stress tests).
- [ ] Merge/rebase safety has proof obligations encoded as tests and invariants (so we don’t accidentally optimize into unsoundness).
